subject: chemistry
title: States of matter and changes of state
key_idea: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. In the particle model, particles are small solid spheres. The stronger the forces between particles, the more energy is needed to change state, so the higher the melting and boiling points.

blocks.text: This section shows how the particle model describes solids, liquids and gases. In the model, particles are small solid spheres.

items.meaning: A simple model in which every particle is a small solid sphere.
The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas.

rows: Can flow, takes the shape of its container

items: A substance can only flow if its particles can move past each other.
Atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of a material. A single atom does not have a melting point.
Solid particles vibrate in fixed positions. Liquid particles move past each other. Gas particles move quickly and are far apart.
Energy and movement increase from solid to liquid to gas.

blocks.text: This section names each change of state and explains it using energy and forces between particles.

diagram.alt: Solid melts to a liquid, which boils to a gas. The reverse changes are condensing and freezing.

items: Solid to liquid is **melting**. Liquid to solid is **freezing**.
Liquid to gas is **boiling** or evaporating. Gas to liquid is **condensing**.
Melting and freezing happen at the melting point. Boiling and condensing happen at the boiling point.
Changes of state are physical changes. No new substance is made.
The change is easily reversed. The particles stay the same, only their arrangement, movement and energy change.
A chemical change makes a new substance and is not easily reversed.
Heating gives particles more energy. At the melting or boiling point they have enough energy to overcome the forces between them.
The stronger the forces between particles, the more energy is needed, so the higher the melting point and boiling point.
The forces depend on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.
Changes of state are physical changes: no new substance is made and they are reversible.
Stronger forces between particles mean higher melting and boiling points.

sections.heading: Predicting states and limits of the model

blocks.text: Data tells you the state of a substance at a given temperature. The particle model is simple, so it has limits.

items.text: Below it, the substance is a solid.
Above it, the substance is a gas.
At or above the melting point and below the boiling point, the substance is a liquid.

diagram.alt: Change the temperature of water and watch the particles change state.

blocks.text: AQA teaches this at Higher tier only. OCR teaches it to all students. Edexcel does not ask for it.

items: The model has no forces between the particles. Real particles attract each other.
All particles are shown as spheres. The spheres are solid and inelastic.
The model does not show the size of particles or the space between them.
Below the melting point a substance is a solid. Above the boiling point it is a gas. In between it is a liquid.
The model ignores forces between particles and shows every particle as a solid sphere.

checks.q: Describe how the particles are arranged and how they move in a solid.
checks.a: The particles are in a regular arrangement, close together, and vibrate in fixed positions.

checks.q: A substance has a melting point of -114 °C and a boiling point of 78 °C. State its physical state at 25 °C and give a reason.
checks.a: Liquid. 25 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point.

checks.q: Explain why a substance with strong forces between its particles has a high melting point.
checks.a: A lot of energy is needed to overcome the strong forces between the particles, so a high temperature is needed to melt it.

exam_phrases: (so) the intermolecular forces are weak
(which) require little energy to overcome
(so) more energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces
above the boiling point of water
the atoms gain energy and their arrangement becomes less ordered
boiling point is a bulk property

mistakes.wrong: Propane has a low boiling point because the covalent bonds are weak.
mistakes.right: Answers about breaking covalent bonds are not accepted. Say the forces between molecules (intermolecular forces) are weak and need little energy to overcome.

mistakes.wrong: The change at the surface of the sea water is boiling.
mistakes.right: Say evaporating or vaporisation for the change from liquid to vapour at the surface. Boiling is not accepted here.

mistakes.wrong: The boiling point of a single bromine molecule is 59 °C.
mistakes.right: Boiling point is a bulk property. It relates to the forces between many molecules, so it is not a property of one molecule.

worked_example.question: Explain why water vapour and not liquid water is produced when diesel burns.
answer_points: Diesel burns at a high temperature, or at a temperature greater than 100 °C.
This is above the boiling point of water, so water is produced as a gas (water vapour).
worked_example.tip: One mark for the high temperature, one for linking it to the boiling point of water.

exam_phrases: no new substance is made
it is reversible
it is only a change of state
regularly arranged / lattice (solid)
randomly arranged / moving (liquid)
evaporation / boiling / vaporisation (liquid to gas)
freezing / solidifying (liquid to solid)

mistakes.wrong: The change from liquid to gas is called the boiling point.
mistakes.right: 'Boiling point' is not accepted. Name the change: evaporation, boiling or vaporisation.

mistakes.wrong: A change of state is a physical change because you can see it.
mistakes.right: 'You can see the change' is ignored. Say no new substance is made and the change is reversible.

mistakes.wrong: Wax is a physical change because no bonds are broken.
mistakes.right: 'No bonds or intermolecular forces are broken' is ignored. Give the two marking points: it is reversible and no new substance is made.

worked_example.question:
The test tube contains solid wax.
As the test tube was heated, the solid wax changed to liquid wax.
After heating, the wax was allowed to cool to room temperature.
When the wax cools, it changes from a liquid back to a solid.
This change is a physical change.

Explain why the change from a liquid to a solid is a physical change rather than a chemical change.
answer_points: It is reversible (or not a permanent change).
No new substance is made (it is only a change of state).
worked_example.tip: One mark for each point. Both ideas must be linked to the change.

exam_phrases: particles move faster in a gas / slower in a solid
particles are further apart in a gas / closer together in a solid
no new substance is made
the change is reversible
it does not take into account forces between particles
it shows all particles as spheres / inelastic
liquid above the melting point and does not boil until the boiling point

mistakes.wrong: In a gas, particles are far apart and move quickly.
mistakes.right: Answers must be comparative when describing a change. Say particles move faster and are further apart in a gas than in a solid.

mistakes.wrong: The particle model is limited because bonds between particles are not shown.
mistakes.right: References to bonds between particles are ignored. Say forces of attraction between particles are not taken into account.
The state alone scores one mark. Give the reason: 25 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point.

worked_example.question:
At –78 °C, and 0.1 MPa pressure, carbon dioxide changes state from a solid to a gas.

Changing state from a solid to a gas is called subliming.

Describe what happens to the movement and arrangement of the particles when a solid turns into a gas. Use the particle model.
answer_points: Particles move faster in a gas and slower in a solid.
Particles have more energy in a gas and less in a solid.
Particles are further apart in a gas and closer together in a solid.
Particles are arranged more randomly in a gas and regularly in a solid.
Forces between particles are weaker in a gas and stronger in a solid.
worked_example.tip: Answers must be comparative. Atoms or molecules can be used for particles.
